title: Reading Input with std::cin
learningObjectives: Recognize the relevant C++ syntax and standard-library convention.
Trace examples and predict their output or behaviour.
Use the topic in a small practical program.
Identify a likely mistake and describe how to avoid it.

understand.concept: The standard input stream std::cin reads data typed or supplied to a program. The extraction operator `>>` stores parsed input into variables. Reading input should be checked because users may provide values of an unexpected type or outside the program's accepted range.
understand.whyItMatters: This concept helps learners write understandable, correct programs and communicate intent to other developers.
understand.analogy: Think of the concept as a clear instruction or label in a workshop that helps everyone use the equipment correctly.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is a guide only; C++ grammar and execution rules define actual behaviour.
understand.explain:
## Reading values
Include `<iostream>` and use `std::cin >> variable`. Extraction commonly skips leading whitespace and reads one token for strings, so it does not read a whole line with spaces.

## Multiple values
You can chain extractions: `std::cin >> first >> second`. Values are read in order.

## Validate input
Check whether extraction succeeded before using the value. For numeric inputs, also validate the accepted range. For full-line text, use `std::getline` and understand how it interacts with earlier formatted input.

examples.title: Read one integer
examples.code: #include <iostream>\nint main(){ int age{}; if(std::cin >> age) std::cout << age << '\\n'; }
examples.explanation: The extraction result is checked before the value is printed.

examples.title: Read two values
examples.code: #include <iostream>\nint main(){ int a{},b{}; if(std::cin >> a >> b) std::cout << a+b << '\\n'; }
examples.explanation: Chained extraction reads two integers in order.

examples.title: Read a token
examples.code: #include <iostream>\n#include <string>\nint main(){ std::string name; if(std::cin >> name) std::cout << name << '\\n'; }
examples.explanation: Formatted extraction into a string reads one whitespace-delimited token.

examples.title: Reject non-numeric input
examples.code: #include <iostream>\nint main(){ int number{}; if(!(std::cin >> number)) std::cout << "Invalid input\\n"; }
examples.explanation: The stream state indicates whether extraction succeeded.

examples.title: Read a whole line
examples.code: #include <iostream>\n#include <string>\nint main(){ std::string line; if(std::getline(std::cin,line)) std::cout << line << '\\n'; }
examples.explanation: getline reads spaces until the line ending.
